moduleTitle: The nature of God as expressed in the Mool Mantra

note.specFocus: Spec 3.1.7.1 Key beliefs: the nature of God as expressed in the Mool Mantra – the content and significance of the Mool Mantra, Guru Granth Sahib (GGS) 1a.
note.summary:
The Mool Mantra ('root verse') is the opening statement of the Guru Granth Sahib, at the top of Ang (page) 1, before Guru Nanak's Japji Sahib. Sikh tradition holds that Guru Nanak first spoke it after his experience of God at the river Bein in Sultanpur (c.1499), when he disappeared for three days and returned saying 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim'. Because it is the root of the scripture, it is recited daily in Nitnem, at the Amrit Sanskar and in many other ceremonies.

CONTENT – each phrase explained
• Ik Onkar – there is One God (the numeral 1 shows absolute oneness). The Ik Onkar symbol is found in gurdwaras, homes and on jewellery.
• Satnam – God's name is Truth; God is eternal reality.
• Karta Purakh – God is the Creator, the 'Creative Being'.
• Nirbhau – without fear; nothing can threaten God.
• Nirvair – without hatred or enmity; God has no enemies.
• Akal Murat – timeless, immortal form; God is beyond time and death.
• Ajuni – beyond birth; God is never born into any form, so Sikhs reject the idea of avatars.
• Saibhang – self-existent; God depends on nothing.
• Gurprasad – known by the Guru's grace; human effort alone cannot reach God.
The lines that follow (often recited with it) say God was 'True in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and will be forever true'.

SIGNIFICANCE
1. It sums up Sikh belief about God – a 'creed' in a few words.
2. It shapes ethics: if God is fearless and without hatred, Sikhs should try to live fearlessly and without hatred; if One God made all, all people are equal.
3. It is used for nam japna (meditation on God's name), helping Sikhs overcome haumai.
4. It marks belonging: the Panj Pyare recite it at Amrit Sanskar; some parents whisper it to a newborn.
5. Many words are negative (without fear, without hatred, unborn), showing that God is beyond full human description – the Japji says God cannot be grasped by thinking, even a hundred thousand times (Ang 1).

DIVERSITY OF VIEW
Some Sikhs say the Mool Mantra ends at 'Gurprasad'; others include the following 'Jap… Aad sach' lines. All Sikhs agree it is the foundation of the scripture, though many stress it must be lived (truthful living, Ang 62), not just recited. Non-religious critics may say its claims cannot be proven.

CONTEMPORARY EXAMPLE
Sikhs worldwide recite the Mool Mantra in the early morning (amrit vela) as part of Japji Sahib; gurdwaras in Britain often display Ik Onkar near the takht; Sikh charities such as Khalsa Aid express 'Nirvair' by helping people of all backgrounds without hatred.

KEY TERMS: Mool Mantra, Ik Onkar, Satnam, Karta Purakh, Nirbhau, Nirvair, Akal Murat, Ajuni, Saibhang, Gurprasad, Ang, Nitnem, Japji Sahib.

questions.question:
Which one of the following words in the Mool Mantra means 'without fear'?
A Nirvair
B Nirbhau
C Ajuni
D Saibhang
questions.modelAnswer: B – Nirbhau. 'Nir' means 'without' and 'bhau' means 'fear'. Nirvair means without hatred/enmity, Ajuni means beyond birth (not born into any life form) and Saibhang means self-existent.
evidence: Mool Mantra, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 1
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one is correct; write the letter clearly. If unsure, cross out options you know are wrong first.

questions.question:
Where is the Mool Mantra found in the Guru Granth Sahib?
A At the start of the Japji Sahib on Ang 1
B In the Rehras Sahib on Ang 8
C In the Kirtan Sohila on Ang 12
D In the Saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur near the end
questions.modelAnswer: A – At the start of the Japji Sahib on Ang 1. The Mool Mantra is the opening statement of the Guru Granth Sahib and stands at the head of Guru Nanak's Japji Sahib. It is also repeated (in full or short form) at the start of many later sections.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one is correct; write the letter clearly. If unsure, cross out options you know are wrong first.

questions.question: Give one quality of God described in the Mool Mantra.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: God is One (Ik Onkar); God's name is Truth (Satnam); God is the Creator (Karta Purakh); God is without fear (Nirbhau); God is without hatred (Nirvair); God is timeless/immortal (Akal Murat); God is beyond birth and death (Ajuni); God is self-existent (Saibhang); God is known by the Guru's grace (Gurprasad).
questions.examTip: A 1-mark short response needs one accurate, relevant point only. A short phrase or sentence is enough; do not waste time explaining.

questions.question: Give one meaning of the term 'Gurprasad' in the Mool Mantra.
questions.modelAnswer: God is known/realised through the Guru's grace (God's grace is needed to understand God).
questions.examTip: A 1-mark short response needs one accurate, relevant point only. A short phrase or sentence is enough; do not waste time explaining.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which the belief that God is One (Ik Onkar) influences Sikhs today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Because Ik Onkar teaches that there is only one God who created and is present in all people, Sikhs treat everyone as equal. This influences them to welcome people of every religion, caste and gender into the gurdwara and to sit them side by side in the langar.

Second way: The Ik Onkar symbol reminds Sikhs that their whole life should be centred on the One God. Many Sikhs display it in their homes and gurdwaras and begin the day by reciting the Mool Mantra in Japji Sahib, so that every activity, including work and family life, is done with God in mind.
evidence: Ik Onkar – the first words of the Mool Mantra, Ang 1
questions.examTip: Give two separate ways. For each, make a simple point (1 mark) and then develop it with an example, consequence or detail (2 marks). Two undeveloped points score only 2.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which the Mool Mantra is important in the daily life of Sikhs.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: It is recited every morning as the opening of Japji Sahib in Nitnem. This means Sikhs start the day by remembering what God is like – true, fearless, without hatred – which focuses their mind on God before work begins.

Second way: It is used at key life events. For example, at the Amrit Sanskar the Panj Pyare recite the Mool Mantra and the initiate repeats it, and some families whisper it to a newborn baby. This shows the Mool Mantra marks belonging to the Sikh community and the start of a God-centred life.

questions.question:
Explain two Sikh teachings about the nature of God as expressed in the Mool Mantra.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Sikh belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First teaching: God is One and is the Creator (Ik Onkar, Karta Purakh). There is only one God, not many gods, and everything in the universe comes from this one source. This means all people and all creation share the same origin, so no group is closer to God by birth.

Second teaching: God is eternal and beyond birth (Akal Murat, Ajuni, Saibhang). God is not born, does not die and depends on nothing else, so Sikhs reject the idea that God takes human form as an avatar. God can be known only through grace (Gurprasad), not by human effort alone.

Source: The Mool Mantra on Ang 1 of the Guru Granth Sahib begins 'Ik Onkar, Satnam, Karta Purakh…' and ends 'Gurprasad'. The lines after it – 'True in the beginning, true throughout the ages, true now… and forever true' – show that God's nature never changes, which supports the teaching that God is eternal.
evidence: 'Aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhi sach, Nanak hosi bhi sach' – Ang 1

Naming the Guru Granth Sahib with an Ang number, or a Guru's teaching, and showing how it supports your point is the safest way to get the source marks.

questions.question:
Explain two reasons why the Mool Mantra is significant for Sikhs.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Sikh belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First reason: It sums up Sikh belief about God in a few words. Tradition holds it was the first teaching of Guru Nanak after his experience at the river Bein, so Sikhs see it as the foundation (mool = root) of all the Guru's teaching that follows in the scripture.

Second reason: It is used for meditation and worship. Repeating the Mool Mantra (and the name Waheguru) is a form of nam japna, which helps Sikhs remember God and overcome haumai (ego), moving them towards mukti.

Source: The Mool Mantra opens the Guru Granth Sahib on Ang 1 and a shortened form is repeated at the start of many sections, which shows how central it is. Its final word 'Gurprasad' teaches that God is known by grace, so Sikhs recite it humbly, asking for that grace.
evidence: Guru Nanak at the river Bein (c.1499)

questions.question:
“The Mool Mantra tells Sikhs everything they need to know about God.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

The Mool Mantra is the first composition in the Guru Granth Sahib (Ang 1) and its name means 'root' teaching. Sikhs believe Guru Nanak received it after his experience of God at the river Bein, so it is revelation. Many Sikhs argue that everything later in the scripture is an expansion of this root, so in principle it contains everything essential.

It covers the most important qualities of God in a carefully ordered way: God is One (Ik Onkar), Truth (Satnam), the Creator (Karta Purakh), without fear or hatred (Nirbhau, Nirvair), timeless, unborn and self-existent (Akal Murat, Ajuni, Saibhang). A Sikh who meditates on these words learns how to relate to God and how to live – fearlessly, without hatred and truthfully.

It also tells Sikhs how God is known: 'Gurprasad' – by the Guru's grace. So it does not just describe God but shows the path to God, which is arguably the most important thing a believer needs.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

The Mool Mantra is very short. It tells Sikhs what God is like, but it does not explain how to escape haumai, what the five khands are, or how to live as gurmukh. These are found in Japji Sahib and the rest of the 1,430 Angs of the Guru Granth Sahib, so Sikhs need the whole scripture, not just its opening.

Many words in the Mool Mantra are negative (without fear, without hatred, beyond birth). They tell Sikhs what God is not rather than giving a full description, which suggests God is ultimately beyond words. The Japji itself says that God cannot be understood by thinking, even if one thinks a hundred thousand times (Ang 1). So no text could tell 'everything' about God.

Sikhs also believe God is experienced, not just known about. Nam japna, sewa and the sangat give an inner experience of God that words cannot replace. A humanist would add that the Mool Mantra makes claims that cannot be tested, so it cannot tell anyone 'everything' about a being whose existence is not proven.

CONCLUSION

The Mool Mantra gives Sikhs everything essential about God in summary form, which is why it is called the root. However, 'everything they need to know' is too strong: Sikh teaching itself says God is beyond full human understanding and must be experienced through grace, meditation and service. The stronger view is that the Mool Mantra is the indispensable foundation, but not the whole building.
evidence: Japji Sahib and the five khands

questions.question:
“Ik Onkar is the most important belief in Sikhism.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Ik Onkar ('There is one God') are the first words of the Mool Mantra and of the whole Guru Granth Sahib (Ang 1). Their position shows that every other teaching depends on them. If God were not One, the other qualities in the Mool Mantra – Creator, Truth, without hatred – would not make sense.

Belief in one God underpins Sikh ethics. Because the One God created everyone and is present in everyone ('Among all is the Light, and You are that Light' – Ang 13), Sikhs believe in the equality of all people, expressed in langar, sangat and the rejection of caste. So Ik Onkar is the source of Sikh social teaching as well as belief.

It is also the basis of worship. Nam japna is meditation on the Name of the one God, and the goal of life, mukti, is union with the One. Without Ik Onkar there would be no aim to Sikh life at all.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

Some Sikhs would say that knowing God is One is not enough – what matters is how a person lives. Guru Nanak taught that 'Truth is higher than everything, but higher still is truthful living' (Ang 62). On this view, sewa, honest work (kirat karna) and sharing (vand chhakna) are just as important, because belief without action does not lead to mukti.

Others might argue that belief in the Guru – God's grace through the Gurus and the authority of the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru – is the most distinctive Sikh belief. Many religions believe in one God, but belief in the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib is what makes Sikhism distinct.

Others might stress becoming gurmukh and overcoming haumai, since this is what Sikhs actually struggle with every day. A non-religious person might argue that the most valuable parts of Sikhism are its ethical values – equality and service – which can be admired without believing in God at all.

CONCLUSION

Although sewa, the Guru and the struggle against haumai are vital, each only makes sense because of Ik Onkar: equality comes from one Creator, the Guru reveals the one God, and haumai is overcome by remembering the one God's Name. So Ik Onkar is best seen as the most important belief because it is the foundation of all the others, even though Sikhs insist it must be lived out, not just believed.
evidence: 'Sabh meh jot jot hai soi' – Ang 13
'Sachahu orai sabh ko upar sach aachaar' – Ang 62
Kirat karna, vand chhakna, nam japna
